Soroban in Various Number Systems

Place ValueCountingArithmetic
Game: A Japanese counting frame. Each bead that touches the middle bar counts; the top bead counts as five ones.
How to play: Click a bead to slide it to the bar or away. Choose another radix to count in other number systems.
Look for the math

The soroban came to Japan from China, probably in the 16th century. A bar divides it into heaven, above, and earth, below. Each wire is one place of a number, the rightmost the units, and the beads touching the bar give that place's digit.

Five is half of ten

On a decimal soroban each wire has one heaven bead worth 5 and four earth beads worth 1 each. That makes every digit from 0 to 9 in exactly one way: 7 = 5 + 1 + 1. (Old sorobans had a fifth earth bead, which was never needed and was dropped around 1920.) The trick works for any even base r: one heaven bead worth r/2 and r/2 − 1 earth beads give each digit from 0 to r − 1 exactly once. The logic test checked this for every base from 2 to 20.

Place value

In base r each wire is worth r times the wire to its right, so the digits d₆ d₅ … d₀ mean d₆r⁶ + … + d₁r + d₀, as in any positional number system. Bases above 10 use letters for the digits 10, 11, … (A, B, …). The line under the frame gives the number in base 10 too.

Trading four ones for a five

When all the earth beads on a wire are up and you push the heaven bead down, the earth beads drop away: four ones are traded for one five (in base r, r/2 − 1 ones for one r/2). This is how the applet behaves. A soroban user does the same with fingers.

Set the radix to 2. With no earth beads at all, the soroban becomes a row of binary switches. What number do all seven heaven beads down make?
